detail.longDescription: arXiv:2611.21620v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern service systems combine rapidly changing dependencies, heterogeneous telemetry, and operational actions whose side effects may amplify an incident. Conventional AIOps research has produced effective detectors, localizers, and diagnostic models, yet surveys typically organize them by task, telemetry modality, or learning technique. Such taxonomies describe what a method predicts, but not which decisions it may make or which evidence justifies that authority. We survey the transition from AIOps pipelines to agentic service operations through three coupled lenses: capability, operational authority, and evaluation evidence. We first relate SOA, microservices, Kubernetes, service meshes, and serverless platforms to the incident lifecycle. We then review conventional AIOps methods and audit 22 language-model-enabled systems according to their evaluated behavior rather than their intended autonomy. The audit shows that most systems remain copilots or read-only investigators. Only two exercise write authority; both use constrained action envelopes, and neither carries controlled production-outcome evidence. Building on these findings, we synthesize a four-plane reference architecture, evidence grades, an evaluation ladder, and a controlled adoption path. Together, these artifacts clarify which claims current evaluations support and what evidence is still required for dependable agentic service operations.
